To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there are substantial differences in the shadow values of crop diversity across Finnish farms; (2) the shadow values of the conventional farms are lower than those of the organic farms; (3) the shadow values are higher in the organic farms than in the conventional farms, and the differences are larger in the case of the more diverse farms; and (4) the shadow values in both types of farming are lower for the more diverse farms.
the opportunity costs of producing crop diversity vary across farms and between organic and conventional farming.

(1) the opportunity cost of producing public goods is higher for organic farms, (2) the opportunity cost is lower in years when crop diversity is higher, and (3) there is a significant variation in the opportunity costs of conservation between farms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the economic efficiency of the production of crop diversity and with the potential of targeted environmental policies to reduce the costs of conservation.
the cost efficiency of conservation and its implications for the design of environmental policy.
the economic efficiency of conservation programs in agriculture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the opportunity cost of providing crop diversity is not high in either organic or conventional farming.
there is no single best way to design conservation payments, but the optimal design depends on the specific characteristics of the farms, the environmental goods, and the conservation programs.
there is variation among the farms and between the farming systems in the shadow values.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shadow prices of producing crop diversity are not high enough to justify a voluntary program.
the opportunity costs of producing crop diversity in organic and conventional farming can be reduced by specialization in the production.
the shadow values of producing public goods in conventional and organic farms vary between farms and that the variation is larger for the organic technology.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there are significant differences in the shadow values of crop diversity between the organic and conventional farming systems, which suggests that environmental policies may need to be targeted at different farming systems to be cost-efficient.
it is possible to estimate the opportunity costs of conservation in a cost-efficient way.
the cost-efficiency in the production of crop diversity varies between organic and conventional farms.
